common_name: McColley's Finale Philodendron (Burgundy New-Growth Self-Heading Philodendron)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; McColley's Finale is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix. McColley's Finale produces new leaves in a deep wine-burgundy that gradually shifts through shades of copper and bronze before settling into a dark green, so an actively growing plant carries several color stages of foliage at once, giving it more seasonal color interest than solidly green self-heading philodendrons. Its compact, non-climbing rosette habit needs no staking or support, making it a manageable tabletop or floor accent depending on pot size. Give it bright, indirect light for the richest new-growth color, since low light dulls the burgundy tones, but keep it out of direct sun, which can scorch the tender young leaves. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix. Autumn produces new leaves in warm copper and burnt-orange tones that pass through gold and olive before maturing to green, echoing the color progression of fall foliage on a plant that lives year-round on a windowsill rather than a deciduous tree, and giving the name its meaning. Like other self-heading philodendrons in its group, it forms a compact, upright, non-climbing rosette that needs no staking, making it a manageable tabletop or floor accent depending on pot size. Give it bright, indirect light for the richest new-growth color, and keep it out of direct sun, which can scorch tender young leaves. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

common_name: Rojo Congo Philodendron (Dark Burgundy Self-Heading Philodendron)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix; Rojo Congo is a compact, self-heading (non-climbing) selection that needs no moss pole or trellis.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio container in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky, humus-rich potting mix. Rojo Congo is a large hybrid philodendron, a cross of Philodendron 'Imperial Red' and 'Black Cardinal', producing big, broad, glossy leaves that emerge coppery red and mature to a deep, near-black burgundy-green, forming a bold, dense, upright rosette without any need to climb. It is the parent of the smaller, more compact 'Birkin' sport, and grows considerably larger than Birkin over time, making a substantial architectural floor specimen in a bright room. Give it bright, indirect light for the darkest, richest leaf color, and keep it out of direct sun, which can scorch the foliage. Let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

common_name: Variegated Clarinervium Anthurium (Variegated Velvet Cardboard Anthurium)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light; requires consistent warmth (65-85°F), high humidity (60-80%), and excellent drainage. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil, never dense potting compost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade, since this collector's form needs adequate light for both leaf health and variegation but will bleach and burn in direct sun. This variegated form of the velvet cardboard anthurium carries irregular patches of cream to pale yellow scattered across the same thick, heart-shaped, deeply veined, dark green velvety leaves that make the species so prized, so each new leaf's variegation pattern is somewhat unpredictable. Because the pale, chlorophyll-poor patches photosynthesize less efficiently than solid green tissue, it grows more slowly and needs slightly brighter light than the plain species to stay vigorous. Water thoroughly when the top layer of the chunky mix dries, since the plant is more drought-tolerant than humidity-tolerant and chronic overwatering causes rapid root rot; all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse specimen in bright indirect light; Anthurium villenaorum requires consistent warmth (65-85°F), high humidity (60-80%), and excellent drainage. Use a chunky, well-aerated epiphytic mix of orchid bark, perlite, and potting soil, never dense potting compost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade in a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix, since this Ecuadorian species needs adequate light for healthy leaf production but will bleach and burn in direct sun. Anthurium villenaorum is a velvet-leaf species with large, heart-shaped, deeply quilted, matte dark green leaves marked by pale, prominently sunken venation, prized by collectors alongside better-known velvet anthuriums like clarinervium and magnificum for its dramatic leaf texture. It is a slower-growing species that rewards patience with increasingly large, more deeply textured leaves as the plant matures. Water thoroughly when the top layer of the potting mix dries, since the plant is more drought-tolerant than humidity-tolerant and chronic overwatering causes rapid root rot; provide consistently warm temperatures and high humidity for the best growth, and note that all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant outdoors as a groundcover in zone 10-11, or grow in shallow pots elsewhere; Predatress has no frost tolerance and is damaged below 35°F. Divide and reset overcrowded clumps every 1-2 years to keep individual rosettes tight and well colored.

directions: Give bright, filtered light or a few hours of gentle morning sun; Predatress colors up darkest and most dramatic with more light exposure, while deep shade fades the rosette toward plain green. Predatress is a striking hybrid Neoregelia with broad, heavily mottled and speckled leaves in blackish-maroon over a paler base color, giving each rosette an intense, almost predatory dappled pattern that stands out sharply against plainer green or solid-colored bromeliads nearby. Like other neoregelias it holds water in its central cup, which should be kept filled and periodically flushed with fresh water to prevent stagnation, and it produces offset pups at the base that can be divided once they have their own roots. Grow in a shallow, fast-draining bromeliad or epiphyte mix, and protect from any frost, since it is strictly a warm-climate or container plant outside zone 10 and warmer.
